item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Pearce+ has added a wildlife tower for bats, owls, kestrels, invertebrates and wetland species at Honeygar Farm in Somerset, UK.

Built almost entirely from reclaimed materials found on the farm, the wildlife tower forms part of a wider plan to restore a wetland habitat on the Somerset Levels.

"The core idea was to create a long-term piece of wildlife infrastructure that could stand the test of time and provide opportunities for as many different species as possible," Pearce+ founding director Owen Pearce told Dezeen.

"It sits within the wider wetland restoration of Honeygar, where Somerset Wildlife Trust is transforming a former farm into restored wetland habitat alongside a new research and education centre."

The tower was designed to become a home for numerous species of animals, which determined its overall form.

"Rather than designing a house for one species, we've tried to create the conditions for lots of different wildlife to move in," said Pearce.

Read:

Invisible Studio & Pearce+ top domed woodworking pavilion with aluminium shingles

"Different species need to nest or roost at particular heights, so the overall height of the tower is partly dictated by the animals it is designed for," he continued.

"Barn owls, for example, naturally seek elevated, protected nesting places. The size of the upper structure is then determined by the dimensions of the different wildlife boxes housed inside it."

The tower was built on masonry piers made from reclaimed materials as the site regularly floods. Above this, the structure was made from reclaimed timber and corrugated metal.

"The idea of the site's restoration informed how we built the tower," said Pearce.

"We wanted to use as few new materials as possible, instead reclaiming materials that were already available on the farm and giving them a new purpose as habitat."

According to Pearce, the process of utilising reclaimed materials added a challenge to the construction process.

"The biggest challenge is the amount of work and uncertainty involved," he said. "Reuse sounds simple but you have to find the materials, dig them out, move them, clean them, assess them and then work out how they can actually be incorporated into the building."

"You can design with an idea of what materials are available, but until you start building there is always an element of the unknown," he continued.

Along with specific spaces for barn owls, kestrels and bats, Pearce hopes that the structure will also become home to a wider variety of wildlife.

"The tower is intended to work at lots of different scales," said Pearce. "Untreated timber can provide habitat for moths, spiders, woodlice and other invertebrates."

"The reclaimed masonry has cracks, textures and cavities that insects and small animals can inhabit, while openings within the piers could be used by amphibians or small mammals. Rubble and earth around the base creates a hibernaculum, a damp habitat that might suit newts, slow worms and other wetland species," he continued.

"We've provided the infrastructure, but ultimately wildlife will decide how to occupy it. In a way, the exciting part is that the building isn't finished when we leave – its inhabitants will complete it."

Previously, Pearce+ created a temporary sub-zero restaurant in Canada and a woodworking shelter at Westonbirt arboretum in Gloucestershire.

The photography is by Samuel Bray.

item.content:encoded:
Designers from IKEA and Xbox were paired up to create the products in this furniture collection, including a stool that looks and tilts like a giant thumbstick.

Unveiled today at the Gamescom fair in Cologne, the nine-piece YXSTABY range is Xbox's debut foray into gaming furniture, designed to blend easily into the home when it's out of action.

"We set out to make furniture people really want in their home, not furniture they accept because it is what you need to game," said IKEA product design developer Philip Dilé.

Each of the pieces in the collection was designed by a team made up of one IKEA designer and one Xbox designer, uniting their gaming and furniture design expertise.

The standout product is a stool modelled on the distinctive thumbsticks found on Xbox controllers.

"We were looking at which objects people actually have around them when they play, and the thumbstick kept looking like a small stool to us," IKEA designer David Wahl told Dezeen.

Adapted from original 3D models of the device, the stool features a curved base that allows it to tilt in all directions much like the real thumbstick, allowing users to lean into the action.

The seat even has the same grippy tessellated edges, now serving to hold the sitter rather than their thumbs in place.

"The challenge wasn't creating a giant thumbstick; the challenge was creating a great stool that still felt like a thumbstick," Xbox design director Elliot Hsu explained.

"We went back to the controller's original design files and spent a lot of time refining the proportions, texture, seating curve and stability. We wanted people to recognize it instantly while still feeling comfortable and functional in a living room."

Other pieces that play on some of Xbox's recognisable design elements include a shiny stainless-steel platter and a cushion in the company's signature shade of green, both shaped to look like the controller's sunken cross-shaped D-pad.

Clever storage is another theme that runs through the collection, often set on casters or equipped with handles so it can easily be moved around the home and turn any room into a game station.

Read:

IKEA unveils inflatable chair that "challenges traditional gaming design"

Most notably, there's IKEA's first go at creating a TV stand since a failed attempt in 2012.

Set on casters, it can be rolled wherever it is needed, while opting for a square over a tubular metal frame keeps it from looking too much like office furniture, explained IKEA designer Lukas Bazle.

"Our focus here was to make a TV stand that's really safe, sturdy and affordable, and that looks good in a lot of different homes," he said.

"Doing a product like that at IKEA is sometimes harder than you'd think. We test our furniture very intensely, and with a TV and castors involved, a lot of things can go wrong."

There's also a wooden toolbox for holding various gaming gear and paraphernalia, which doubles as a laptop stand, as well as a rolling side table with integrated charging stations and a lounge chair with hidden storage pockets below the seat.

Its bouncy, cantilevered design was conceived to support both active and leisurely play.

"I hadn't thought at all about people playing in different modes," Bazle said.

"You sit forward when the game needs your full attention, and then there are games you play to relax, where you're sunk into the chair, and it's a completely different way of sitting. The lounge chair had to handle both."

The pieces are rendered in timber and muted neutrals of black, white and grey, with splashes of green guiding the eye to the integrated storage.

IKEA has gone full-force on gaming furniture in recent years, with previous launches including an inflatable gaming chair and a range of high-tech desks and chairs with Republic of Gamers.

Developer Riksbyggen and creative agency BBDO Nordics have designed three flats based on what a 25-year-old can afford to buy in Sweden today, with the smallest micro home measuring just 1.9 square metres.

The sizes of the three apartments were based on Riksbyggen's square metre index, which calculates how many square metres of housing a young person can afford based on income, property prices and mortgage conditions.

The calculations were made using data from government agency Statistics Sweden (SCB) and digital bank Avanza.

Riksbyggen and BBDO Nordics looked at incomes in three Swedish cities – Stockholm, Gothenburg and Umeå – to create a broad geographical spread when calculating the size of the homes, which the companies are calling Sweden's smallest apartments.

"Stockholm, Gothenburg and Umeå are among the Swedish cities where young people have a particularly strong need for housing, while also facing significant difficulties finding and affording it," BBDO Nordics art director Anton Bolin told Dezeen.

"Together, the three cities show that the issue affects young people across Sweden, from south to north."

After calculating what a 25-year-old with the national average income and savings could afford to buy in each city, the companies designed three tiny apartments: one measuring 1.9 square metres for Stockholm, a 3.1-square-metre flat for Gothenburg and a 4.5-square-metre home for Umeå.

"The idea is to make the housing crisis facing young people visible and tangible," Bolin said. "We see numbers and statistics about it everywhere, but they can easily become abstract."

"So we wanted to show exactly how much home an average 25-year-old can afford today, and let people experience that reality."

Bolin then worked with Bengt Svedlund from Stockholm company Dekormakarna to create the three flats, which were designed to look typically Swedish.

"We wanted the houses to look like typical Swedish homes, the kind of houses you see all over the country," Bolin said. "With familiar architecture and details, but at an unusual scale that makes the absurdity of the situation immediately clear."

Each of the three buildings has a distinctive design, ranging from more classical building types to contemporary housing.

"The first is inspired by turn-of-the-century style, with a rendered facade in 'Stockholm yellow', herringbone flooring, mullioned windows and ceiling mouldings," Bolin explained.

Read:

Eight innovative micro homes that make small sites feel big

"The second draws on 1930s/40s functionalism, with clean lines, light pastel colours, linoleum flooring and a corrugated metal balcony," he continued.

"The third represents contemporary housing, with a brick facade and simpler, more functional materials."

One in five young people in Sweden still live with their parents, according to Bolin, who hopes that the project will ultimately help to rally public support for more affordable housing.

"We hope the project gets more people talking about the problem and puts housing higher on the political agenda," he said.

"That's why we launched the project ahead of Sweden's general election in September 2026. Our hope is that the next government will take action on the three housing reforms we believe are needed."

Previous micro homes featured on Dezeen include a house in a former wind turbine and an "aspirational" housing prototype in India.

The photography is by Jörgen Brennicke from Rockson.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Colar has updated and extended a dilapidated adobe structure to create a single-storey home in Chiapas, Mexico.

Named Casa Estelí, the 162-square-metre dwelling combines the revived adobe structure with two new brick volumes, each sheltered beneath an expansive, self-supporting timber roof.

Colar centred the project around preserving the existing adobe structure, which involved securing its 30-centimetre-thick walls with vertical reinforcements and a continuous timber beam to ensure its seismic resilience.

To further extend its lifespan, the timber roof is structurally independent to avoid additional loads and complete with overhangs to protect the walls from erosion.

"The main challenge was adapting an existing adobe structure – whose original construction and structural behaviour were not fully known – to new uses without compromising its stability, particularly in relation to seismic demands," the studio told Dezeen.

"The independent timber roof then became a unifying element, connecting the original adobe structure with the two new brick volumes."

To complement the earthy tones of the adobe structure, the two new volumes were built using locally produced clay bricks with a wall thickness of 26 centimetres to match the existing structure.

The masonry was left exposed across the home's exterior and interior, where the use of brick is complemented by a pared-back material palette of exposed timber and clay flooring.

Read:

Al Borde Arquitectos uses adobe for "biosecure" laboratory in Ecuador

"We chose materials that could establish continuity with the existing adobe while remaining clearly distinguishable from it," Colar explained.

"The ochre tones and shared earth-based materiality create a connection between the adobe and brick, while the rat-trap bond provides insulation and a wall thickness close to that of the original construction."

At the home's front, the renewed adobe structure opens up from a spacious verandah to an open-plan living and dining area lit by clerestory openings.

Situated off the living area is the smaller of the two new brick volumes, which contains a study, bathroom and utility space.

Meanwhile, at the home's opposite end, an open-air corridor links to the larger extension, which accommodates the home's two bedrooms and a shared bathroom finished in glossy green tiles.

Elsewhere in Mexico, Studio Font has perched a cliffside home on a series of inhabitable concrete columns and L-shaped roofs top the four volumes that make up a house in Los Cabos.

The photography is by Ariadna Polo.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: US technology company Dell has incorporated Nvidia GPUs and AI-assisted visualisation technologies into its workstation portfolio to support its latest real-time design studio.

According to Dell, advances in graphics processing unit (GPU) rendering and AI-assisted visualisation technologies are helping to close the gap between initial design concepts and final client-ready presentations.

The company noted that real-time workflows are changing the way design studios work, enabling teams to create photorealistic images and explore multiple options interactively.

It also allows studios to test ideas and design iterations as 3D models are updated.

Dell also suggested that "visualisation is becoming part of the design thinking itself". This marks a shift from it being a specialist output at the presentation stage to being a tool for concept development and decision-making during the design process.

"The role of the visualisation specialist has been democratised to the role of the actual designer," Dell AECO alliances and solutions director Ken Flannigan told Dezeen.

To support these workflows, the Dell Pro Max and Dell Pro Precision workstations are equipped with the latest Blackwell generation of Nvidia RTX PRO GPUs.

These professional GPUs combine traditional ray-tracing hardware (RT Cores) with AI-processing capabilities (Tensor Cores).

The Dell Pro Max and Dell Pro Precision workstations support Nvidia's Deep Learning Super Sampling (DLSS) – an AI-assisted technology using pre-trained models to upscale images rendered at a lower resolution, generate additional frames, and improve ray-traced image quality.

According to Flannigan, this represents a change from relying primarily on increasingly powerful hardware towards combining GPU performance with AI-assisted processing.

"Now it's not just power – it's power plus these pre-trained AI intelligent models that are allowing you to work faster," Flannigan said.

"It's not that the GPU got faster, but that the intelligence behind the GPU got better," he added.

Flannigan noted that these advances may also improve energy efficiency by reducing power consumption and heat generation.

By processing visualisations and AI workloads locally on workstations instead of cloud-based services, Dell also suggested that studios can benefit from quicker workflows while maintaining more control over their design data.

Dell argued that while cloud-based services are important for storage and collaboration, local compute can be more predictable in terms of operational costs, as well as for intellectual property protection and data governance requirements.

"Bringing it locally means that you're buying compute, not renting compute," added Flannigan.

He noted this can benefit architecture firms working with sensitive project information and client data, which cannot always be processed through centralised cloud services.

Looking to the future, Flannigan noted that local computing will become increasingly important as design firms begin training AI tools on their own data.

"If we're all training visualisation and design aesthetics on a centralised data source, everything in the future designed by AI will eventually look exactly the same," stated Flannigan.

"So it's really important for designers to own their AI-trained design aesthetic," he added.

item.content:encoded:
Miami voters have approved Denver-based real estate company Oak View Group's bid to take over management of the city's historic Miami Marine Stadium and restore the structure.

Built in 1963 and designed by Cuban architect Hilario Candela, the concrete modernist stadium was closed in 1992 following damage from Hurricane Andrew and has sat abandoned for decades as the city and residents debated its fate.

The City of Miami put forth a special election on 18 August as part of the city's primary race, which included a referendum on a management agreement with Global Spectrum LP, a subsidiary of Oak View Group.

The referendum proposes that the group would oversee the activation and events at Miami Marine Stadium and its surrounding site, including a nearby marina and the proposed Flex Park for the area, with plans to transform the structure "into a reimagined state-of-the-art venue".

In a sample ballot, the referendum also states a 40-year term lease, and that Global Spectrum would pay the city up to $10 million towards the restoration of "the historic Marine Stadium". According to BoatingIndustry, there would be no cost to taxpayers.

Local group Breakwater Hospitality Group is also part of the management deal.

More than 68 per cent of voters approved the referendum.

"We are elated that the Miami community advanced this important step forward in the restoration of one of Miami's most treasured landmarks," said Oak View Group president of venue management Greg O'Dell in a statement issued by the team. "Miami Marine Stadium is more than a venue; it's a symbol of Miami's vibrant history and future."

Read:

Eleven architecture preservation battles across the US

"Alongside our Miami-based partners, Breakwater Hospitality Group, we aim to support the city of Miami in honoring its legacy while creating a vibrant space that will serve generations to come, celebrate local culture, and drive economic growth across the region."

The stadium's restoration is one part of a larger $80 million initiative to modernise and redevelop parts of the surrounding Virginia Key, a spit of land that sits in Biscayne Bay south of Miami Beach.

According to advocacy group Bring Back Marine Stadium and Breakwater Hospitality Group, next steps include "a comprehensive study and visioning process for the renovated stadium" by Oak View Group, who are set to work closely with the City, preservation partners, the community, and Miami's creative and business leaders on the project.

Contract negotiations for the management of Flex Park will also begin.

The team says the project will be "one of the city's most ambitious cultural revitalisation projects in decades".

This is not the first time the city and public have sought to support the resurrection of Miami Marine Stadium.

In 2016, Heineken and the National Trust for Historic Preservation hosted a crowdfunding campaign aimed at raising money for its restoration and conservation group Docomomo listed the structure as one of the most under-threat buildings in the US in 2022.

The photography is by Rick Bravo

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a light made from organic waste from traditional Chinese medicine is among the projects by students at Politecnico di Milano.

Also featured is a modular mycelium habitat for sparrows, and materials made from salmon bones, skin and scales sourced from Japanese restaurants.

Politecnico di Milano

Institution: Politecnico di Milano, Design Department – Poli.Design
Course: Materials Design for Transition
Tutors: Valentina Rognoli, Sofia Soledad Duarte Poblete, Chengjun Li, Ziqian Yu, Malu Luecking and Francesco Cianfano, with the support of the Madetrans research group

School statement:

"Materials Design for Transition (Madetrans) is a research group based at the Department of Design of Politecnico di Milano.

"Founded in 2015 around the DIY-materials approach and led by Valentina Rognoli, the group investigates materials design as a central design practice, positioning its work at the intersection of sustainability, ecology, biodesign and regeneration.

"Its activities are also supported by the Biodesign Lab (B.Lab), the first laboratory dedicated to biodesign within the department of design.

"Through materials-driven and material-centred approaches, Madetrans develops theoretical frameworks, educational methods and hands-on experiments that foster new cultures of materiality.

"The group encourages designers to move beyond exclusively human-centred perspectives towards more-than-human and multispecies approaches, recognising ecosystems, living organisms and their interdependencies as active participants in design processes.

"Its interdisciplinary team brings together industrial and product designers, design engineers and fashion-system specialists, contributing diverse perspectives on material intelligence and its role in sustainable and regenerative futures.

"This selection presents ten student projects developed across courses in materials-driven design and biodesign. Through experimentation, speculation and applied proposals, they embody Madetrans' vision of materials design for transition and highlight an emerging field rooted in interdisciplinary collaboration, ecological thinking, biodesign and nature-driven innovation for broader systemic impact."

Reclaym by Anastasia Prozorova, Ivanna Harulia, Giulia Fabro and Marta Figueiredo

"Reclaym transforms discarded brick waste into a versatile material that combines structural resilience with tactile and aesthetic expression.

"Reclaimed bricks are pulverised into fine powder and mixed with different binders and aggregates to explore new formulations, textures and sensory qualities.

"The resulting samples retain the strength and memory of the original material while appearing unexpectedly soft, light or fragile.

"By inviting touch and challenging visual assumptions, the project reframes construction waste as a medium for creativity rather than merely a sustainable substitute.

"Reclaym demonstrates how reclaimed brick can bridge functionality, material experience and artistic experimentation in contemporary design and architecture."

Students: Anastasia Prozorova, Ivanna Harulia, Giulia Fabro and Marta Figueiredo
Course: Towards Regenerative Materials Driven Futures: Biodesign and Nature-Inspired Solutions
Tutors: Valentina Rognoli, Sofia Soledad Duarte Poblete, Malu Luecking and Francesco Cianfano

Mycelli by Golab Aminialiabadi, Rocco Carraro, Brigitte Guarneri, Keren Karsa, Shyam KS and Elena Pellegrini

"Mycelli explores mycelium as a responsive living material and a temporary interface for urban regeneration.

"Developed through observation, experimentation and material-led decision-making, the project embraces growth, unpredictability and multispecies interaction rather than imposing predetermined forms.

"It proposes a modular mycelium habitat integrated into architectural facades to support declining Italian sparrow populations in Milan.

"Designed for a six-month lifespan, the structure provides nesting space before gradually decomposing, after which its fibrous material can be reused by birds.

"By combining thermal, acoustic and electromagnetic performance with ecological function, Mycelli reframes architecture as a temporary mediator within regenerative urban ecosystems and multispecies coexistence."

Students: Golab Aminialiabadi, Rocco Carraro, Brigitte Guarneri, Keren Karsa, Shyam KS and Elena Pellegrin
Course: Towards Regenerative Materials Driven Futures: Biodesign and Nature-Inspired Solutions
Tutors: Valentina Rognoli, Sofia Soledad Duarte Poblete, Malu Luecking and Francesco Cianfano

Whynut by Nicole Dalle Molle, Giulia Luppi, Selma Wittermann and Mrunal Deshpande

"This project investigates nutshell waste as a resource for circular material systems.

"Through material characterisation and iterative experimentation, different formulations and processing methods were tested to assess structural, tactile and aesthetic qualities.

"The resulting composite showed rigidity, texture and surface characteristics comparable to wood-based materials, suggesting applications as a decorative finish.

"Beyond material development, the project proposes a regenerative system linking food production, waste collection, processing and furniture restoration.

"Rather than creating new objects, it upcycles existing furniture by replacing worn components with nutshell-based surfaces, preserving embedded value while reducing virgin material use, extending product lifespans and minimising further waste."

Students: Nicole Dalle Molle, Giulia Luppi, Selma Wittermann and Mrunal Deshpande
Course: Materials x Transition in the Master of Design for Sustainability and Regeneration
Tutors: Sofia Soledad Duarte Poblete and Valentina Rognoli

Orma by Ines Ravagnani, Gülsüm Koç, Carloalberto Dusi and Mete Sürmeli

"Orma reimagines pine needles, an abundant by-product of agriculture and timber production, as a valuable material resource.

"Through a materials-driven design process combining experimentation, material characterisation, research and documentation, the team developed a biocomposite whose properties ranged from leather-like flexibility to rubber-like resilience.

"These qualities led to the design of a bio-based, biodegradable footwear outsole that addresses the microplastic pollution generated by conventional soles.

"Rather than leaving persistent traces, Orma is conceived to return safely to natural cycles after use.

"The project demonstrates how overlooked waste streams can inspire material innovation while connecting circularity, performance and responsible product design in practice."

Students: Ines Ravagnani, Gülsüm Koç, Carloalberto Dusi and Mete Sürmeli
Course: Materials x Transition in the Master of Design for Sustainability and Regeneration
Tutors: Sofia Soledad Duarte Poblete and Valentina Rognoli

Trice by Josephine Plaum, Juliette Desertot, Matilde Reviglio and Nicola Sdrubolini

"Trice transforms rice-production by-products, including husk, bran, starch, fibre and broken grains, into 100 per cent compostable biomaterials without external binders.

"By combining the structural strength of rice husk with the binding properties of bran, the project develops materials that can be produced locally across rice-growing regions worldwide.

"Its prototypes demonstrate versatility, from rigid packaging components such as boxes and edge protectors to flexible bioplastic films for sealing.

"By redirecting residues that are often burned or underused, Trice closes loops within the rice value chain, reduces pollution and creates economic value while allowing materials to return safely to soil."

Students: Josephine Plaum, Juliette Desertot, Matilde Reviglio and Nicola Sdrubolini
Course: Materials x Transition in the Master of Design for Sustainability and Regeneration
Tutors: Sofia Soledad Duarte Poblete and Valentina Rognoli

Scravita by Chuyue Zhang, Junshuo Cui, Keyan Wu, Mingsheng Li, Kevin Yang, Yifei Li, Yuwei Ma, Jinghui Zhou and Chencheng Liu

"Scravita transforms salmon bones, skin and scales collected from local Japanese restaurants into a family of regenerative materials and a final lighting application.

"Through cleaning, enzymatic treatment, grinding, gelatin extraction and thermal modification, the project explores the structural, translucent and fluorescent qualities of seafood by-products.

"Material experiments combine salmon bone powder, skin-derived gelatin and heat-treated scales with natural binders to achieve different levels of hardness, flexibility and transparency.

"The resulting Salmorph lamp integrates these materials into a softly glowing cube, where fluorescent scales animate the surface under light.

"Scravita reframes seafood waste as a resource for circular, sensory and materially expressive product design."

Students: Chuyue Zhang, Junshuo Cui, Keyan Wu, Mingsheng Li, Kevin Yang, Yifei Li, Yuwei Ma, Jinghui Zhou and Chencheng Liu
Course: Materials for Product Design and Innovation
Tutors: Valentina Rognoli, Zhang Yu, Chengjun Li and Ziqian Yu

LumiStudio by Hu Yi, JiahaoHuang, Yumeng Li, Jiaxin Guo, Yanting Gao, Hanyu Wang, Wanming Feng, Youyou Li, Xindi Yang and Wenjun Ma

"LumiStudio transforms discarded flower tea residues collected from teahouses, restaurants and tea-processing sources in Xi'an into a series of translucent decorative materials.

"Through controlled experiments, the team explored butterfly pea, chrysanthemum, rose and lavender waste, adjusting binders, heating methods, moulds and drying conditions to preserve their natural colours, fibres and textures.

"The final pendant lamp combines selected samples with cotton threads, acrylic elements and 3D-printed supports.

"Illuminated from within, the suspended material pieces reveal varied translucency, surface detail and colour, presenting flower tea waste as an expressive resource for circular product design."

Students: Hu Yi, JiahaoHuang, Yumeng Li, Jiaxin Guo, Yanting Gao, Hanyu Wang, Wanming Feng, Youyou Li, Xindi Yang and Wenjun Ma
Course: Materials for Product Design and Innovation
Tutors: Valentina Rognoli, Zhang Yu, Chengjun Li and Ziqian Yu

Reshelled by Tian Bingxin, Li Ziyu, Chen Xinyue, Li Hongxi, Chen Sixiao, Fan Mingyan, Zhang Baoqi, Tu Yurong, Yu Siyuan and Wang Chongwen

"Reshelled transforms discarded seafood shells collected in Weihai into mineral-based materials for lighting design.

"The team processed shells from different species into particles of varying sizes and combined them with multiple binders to tune their strength, surface texture, colour and translucency.

"Further experiments focused on isolating the iridescent nacreous layer inside abalone shells. Vinegar was used to gradually dissolve the outer shell, revealing a clean and highly reflective inner layer.

"By refining particle distribution, moulding methods and material formulations, the project produced durable, glossy and light-transmitting samples.

"Two lamp prototypes demonstrate how shell waste can replace conventional decorative panels while retaining its natural lustre and marine character."

Students: Tian Bingxin, Li Ziyu, Chen Xinyue, Li Hongxi, Chen Sixiao, Fan Mingyan, Zhang Baoqi, Tu Yurong, Yu Siyuan and Wang Chongwen
Course: Materials for Product Design and Innovation
Tutors: Valentina Rognoli, Zhang Yu, Chengjun Li and Ziqian Yu

Osteomangus by Chen Zhang, He Mengfu, Li Yushuo, Sun Langjun, Zhao Qiyue, Li Yiming, Ni Zhenran, Cao Zhanchang, Sheng Xia and Li Kaifen

"Osteomangus explores chicken bones and mango pits as complementary waste resources for experimental material development.

"Chicken bones collected from a food-processing company in Shandong were cleaned, oxidised, dried and ground into mineral-rich powder, while mango pits sourced from local fruit vendors in Xi'an were processed into natural fibres.

"The team combined these components with gelatin, agar, starch, sodium alginate, mineral fillers and plant fibres to produce a diverse material library.

"Thirteen documented recipes range from flexible, translucent sheets to foamed, leather-like and rigid composites.

"Presented as a material cookbook, Osteomangus provides reproducible formulations while demonstrating the aesthetic and functional potential of agricultural and food-processing residues."

Students: Chen Zhang, He Mengfu, Li Yushuo, Sun Langjun, Zhao Qiyue, Li Yiming, Ni Zhenran, Cao Zhanchang, Sheng Xia and Li Kaifen
Course: Materials for Product Design and Innovation
Tutors: Valentina Rognoli, Zhang Yu, Chengjun Li and Ziqian Yu

Farewell Flower Goddess by Zhaoyu Chen, Kangrui Chen, Xuming Zhu, Boyu Zhan, Huanxu An, Hanzhi Xu, Yanqiao Peng, Xuhan Zhu, Zi'ang Wang and Fang Shi

"Farewell Flower Goddess transforms organic waste from traditional Chinese medicine into translucent sheet materials for lighting design.

"The team collected herbal residues from a local traditional Chinese medicine hospital in Xi'an and investigated how these discarded materials could be recovered as a design resource.

"Through repeated formulation and casting experiments, they addressed brittleness, excessive thickness, poor ductility and curling by adding starch, controlling sheet thickness and testing different herbal mixtures.

"Poria produces a pale, fibrous surface that gently diffuses light, while goji berry creates a warm amber-red glow. The final hexagonal lantern demonstrates how locally sourced medical waste can support circular material development and sensory product design."

Students: Zhaoyu Chen, Kangrui Chen, Xuming Zhu, Boyu Zhan, Huanxu An, Hanzhi Xu, Yanqiao Peng, Xuhan Zhu, Zi'ang Wang and Fang Shi
Course: Materials for Product Design and Innovation
Tutors: Valentina Rognoli, Zhang Yu, Chengjun Li and Ziqian Yu

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio KFA plans to convert a 1970s brutalist office in Los Angeles into housing after its recent designation as a historic landmark, taking advantage of a recently adopted adaptive reuse ordinance.

KFA's plans include converting the stepped concrete building in the city's Sherman Oaks neighbourhood into 95 apartments and turning its former laboratory and printing space into amenities.

The 165,00-square-foot building was designed in the 1970s by AC Martin & Associates to serve as the corporate headquarters of growers' cooperative Sunkist Growers.

Owned and operated by local developer IMT Residential since 2013, the building has been empty since 2015, following Sunkist Growers' relocation.

Following the building becoming vacant, IMT Residential enlisted architecture studio Johnson Fain to restore the structure and update it for seismic resilience.

Johnson Fain also designed a masterplan for the site along with several new buildings on the 8.3-acre site, now known as Citrus Commons.

Recently the building achieved Historic-Cultural Monument status from the City of Los Angeles and the developer plans to utilise recent changes in the city's Adaptive Reuse Ordinance (ARO) to convert the Sunkist building into residential.

According to Los Angeles City Planning, the updated ordinance grants exemptions to certain zoning requirements and reviews and expands the applicable area beyond the city's downtown.

Read:

Logic transforms bland commercial office into "humble and collaborative" workspace

IMT Residential selected KFA to carry out the building's conversion partly due to the studio's role in forwarding Los Angeles' first ARO in 1999.

According to the developer, the conversion will take advantage of its high ceilings to create residential units that range from studios to three-bedroom apartments. Under current zoning, the minimum square footage of a new residence is 450 and IMT Residential cited the smallest for this project at 516 square feet.

On the podium floor, the design will keep the mezzanines, integrating them into the apartments.

"Through adaptive reuse, Citrus Commons demonstrates how reimagined historic buildings can serve future generations while preserving iconic architecture," said IMT Residential in a press release.

The developer plans to begin construction as soon as KFA's plans are approved by the city.

Other conversions of brutalist office buildings include Becker + Becker's conversion of a Marcel Breuer structure in Connecticut into Hotel Marcel and OFIS Arhitekti's conversion of brutalist printworks in Slovenia into offices.

item.content:encoded:
Local architecture practice Studio Massimo has completed a bio-based office in the Netherlands, using bark cladding and an expansive green roof to disguise its form within the surrounding woodland.

Named Office in Nature, the 1,120-square-metre building replaces a derelict events hall on the Tafelberg heath, a protected landscape in North Holland.

According to Amsterdam-based Studio Massimo, the design drew on a historic form of dwelling known as a plaggenhut – homes made by labourers in the region using turf and grass – to create something that would act as an extension of the landscape.

"The atmosphere of the site is genuinely inspiring," the studio's founder Max Verhoeven told Dezeen.

"You feel the millennia of glacial formation, the sand, the heather, the trees shaped by wind. It is magical, and we were very conscious that it should be handled with care, in the design and during construction."

"The building goes beyond disappearing into the heath," he continued. "The roof is an active heather landscape in its own right, planted with around a hundred native, organically grown species. It adds habitat rather than taking it."

On approach from the north, the building's overgrown green roof and a low wall made from repurposed tiles make it almost entirely invisible, save for a path framed by a geometric wooden wall.

Once inside, the building opens up around a seven-metre-high central space, with gabled ceilings lined in pale timber battens that gently curve around the edge of roof lights that run along the entire apex.

Focusing on the use of bio-based materials, the structure of the building was created using laminated timber columns and beams, and its interiors – from walls and ceilings to cupboards and staircases – are finished almost entirely in Red Grandis wood.

Contrasting its hidden northern facade, the southern side of the building projects towards the surrounding heathland with full-height sliding glass doors that provide the offices with panoramic views.

Read:

BIG arranges circular Dymak HQ around stepped courtyard

This elevation, as well as Office in Nature's large gable ends, have been clad entirely in panels of textured poplar bark that blend with the trunks of the surrounding trees.

Above, two cut-outs in the southern slope of the roof create terraces for additional meeting rooms and workspaces on the first floor.

"Every working space has direct sliding-door access to outside: the south nature garden, the west terrace, or the first-floor terraces. Always a direct view of natural life unfolding, always a door to it," Verhoeven said.

"Every technical indication, ventilation grilles, smoke detectors, is minimised or hidden, so the interior stays a peaceful frame for the natural backdrop or other pieces of art, which supply all the life the space needs."

Other projects in the Netherlands recently featured on Dezeen include a pair of interlocking homes in Utrecht by Woonpioniers and a demountable timber library in Amsterdam.

item.content:encoded:
Designer Simon Weckert has created a colourful camouflage shirt that cannot be detected using AI video systems.

Developed in response to a pilot project to use artificial intelligence (AI) video surveillance at Berlin's Kottbusser Tor, which starts this month, the shirt was designed to stop the user being recognised as a person.

Named Digital Camouflage, the shirt aims to confuse the AI-powered object-detection system by subverting what the system recognises as a person.

"AI systems are made of multiple layers and never learned what a human is – they learned what humans statistically look like in millions of training images," said Weckert.

"In the early layers it's edges, contrasts and texture gradients; deeper in the network it's part-like patterns: the head-and-shoulders silhouette, the proportions of limbs against a torso, the continuity of a body's outline against the background," he continued.

"A 'person', for the machine, is a bundle of visual statistics – and that is exactly its weakness."

The shirt uses a combination of bright colours and patterns to confuse the AI systems so that it doesn't recognise what it is seeing as a person.

"Both [colour and pattern], and neither alone – it's their interplay, optimised against the machine rather than the human eye," said Weckert.

Read:

Cap_able blocks facial recognition software with knitted clothing

"The saturated colour transitions fire strongly in the network's early layers, while the overlapping shapes break the continuity of the body's outline, so the detector can no longer bind the parts into one figure," he continued.

"The pattern essentially shouts over the quiet statistical whisper that says 'person'. To a human it reads as an almost hypnotic textile; to the AI model it reads as nothing at all."

Weckert developed the pattern on the shirt using AI. He tested iterations using an AI version of trial and error known as an "adversarial loop".

"The pattern was developed in an adversarial loop with the detection system itself: generate a candidate, show it to the detector, measure how confidently it still finds the person, adjust, repeat – until the confidence collapses," said Weckert.

"This was necessary because a machine's blind spots are not intuitive to humans; you cannot design against machine perception by eye, only the machine can tell you what it fails to see. There's a poetic symmetry in that: the same class of AI that watches the square also taught the shirt how to hide."

Weckert tested the shirt using Yolo, an open-source, real-time AI object detection system.

Another piece of clothing that was tested using Yolo was a piece of knitwear that protects the wearer's biometric data without the need to cover their face.

The photography is by Simon Weckert.

item.description:

item.content:encoded:
The world's most prominent architecture studios are embracing AI for everything from coming up with designs to project analyses and reports, Dezeen research has found.

Twenty-six leading architecture studios from around the world told Dezeen about their use of artificial intelligence (AI), including SOM and Foster + Partners. A further 27 declined to comment or did not reply when approached.

Of the 26 studios that spoke to Dezeen, 25 were not only using AI but actively encouraging it.

Among them are UK firms ZHA and Heatherwick Studio, US studio HOK, Rotterdam-based OMA, Indian studio Morphogenesis, Norwegian studio Snøhetta and Chinese studio MAD.

"In the last two years, the computing power and level of sophistication of AI has grown exponentially," MAD associate partner Tiffany Dahlen told Dezeen.

"As designers, we need to embrace the technology and use it just like any other software or skill to be developed," she continued.

"It's pretty obvious that AI is the major technological change today – just like the shift from hand drafting to CAD to Revit – and we need to learn how to use it to our advantage, otherwise we will be left behind."

Studios encouraging "responsible" use of AI

"HOK actively encourages responsible AI use in all aspects of the firm, in adherence with two complementary firm-wide policies: an AI Authorized Use policy, which specifies how AI may be used, and an AI Governance policy, which defines the ways in which the firm actively manages our AI-related efforts," HOK senior principal Matt Breidenthal told Dezeen.

Others struck a more cautious tone, such as Danish architecture firm CF Møller.

"We are encouraging them to use it, but thoughtfully," said studio partner Rune Bjerno Nielsen.

"Depending on the department or daily role, AI can be less or more beneficial. We try to only use it if it can make an actual impact. Otherwise it gets too expensive, and we also need to look at the environmental impact of data centres."

Barcelona-based Bofill Taller de Arquitectura was the only studio we approached that is not actively using AI, but did not explain why and did not respond to follow-up questions.

Claude.ai among favourite AI tools

The RIBA's now-annual AI survey has identified a steady increase in adoption of the technology by UK architecture studios in the past few years – but our research identified which of the world's top studios are using it, and which tools they tend to prefer.

A clear favourite among the AI tools being adopted is Claude.ai, a large language model (LLM) built by US company Anthropic, which is being used by 44 per cent of the studios we spoke to.

Other popular tools used by the studios include Google's LLM, Gemini, used by eight of the studios, alongside Microsoft Copilot and ChatGPT, each used by 24 per cent of the studios.

For image generation, Gemini's Nano Banana proved the most popular, used by seven of 25 the studios. Stable Diffusion and xFigura were also among most-mentioned image generation tools, used by 12 per cent of the studios.

Read:

Realistic AI architectural renderings must be labelled under EU AI Act

A key trend emerging alongside the use of these AI tools is the development of in-house AI systems, favoured for their personalisation and data privacy.

More than half of the studios that told us they are using AI have created in-house systems, including Foster + Partners, Hassell, Heatherwick Studio, MVRDV, OMA and Gensler.

Notably, despite enthusiastic adoption of AI at many studios, only 19 confirmed that they have established AI policies.

"Yes we do have a policy: we think it's really important to set clear guidelines for responsible use of AI on projects and more widely across our business," Hawkins Brown COO Alastair Roberts said.

"The guidelines cover professional integrity issues like accuracy and confidentiality and also wider issues like bias and environmental impact," he added.

"Ultimately we're stressing that AI produces useful inputs for our work – e.g. it can accelerate or automate some processes very effectively – but we are all still responsible as qualified human professionals for what we deliver to our clients."

Data privacy a concern for studios using AI

Other studios with policies in place cited data privacy as a primary concern.

"Our focus is on giving teams clear guidance around both the opportunities and the risks – particularly around data handling – while still allowing room for experimentation," ZHA director Nils Fischer and Shajay Bhooshan said.

"We have developed a formal AI Policy designed to safeguard the practice in relation to data, confidentiality and intellectual property," Foster + Partners' Martha Tsigkari and Sherif Eltarabishy told Dezeen.

"This allows us to work with AI securely at scale."

At Heatherwick Studio, an AI policy and framework was the second step in its AI strategy, following the creation of an AI working group that assesses the "risks and opportunities" of using AI.

"One of the first steps in our strategy was delivering on a policy, which really focused on ethical use, transparency and integrity, quality assurance, intellectual property, data privacy, and general user concerns around the technology," Heatherwick Studio's director of applied research and AI Pablo Zamorano told Dezeen.

Six studios, including MAD, did not report having an AI policy in place, despite encouraging their architects to use the technology.

"We don't have a formal policy in place yet, but we are encouraging our employees to integrate AI into our daily workflow," MAD's Dahlen said.

AI used to offload "repetitive processes" and administrative tasks

Among the studios using AI, outsourcing the repetitive administrative tasks associated with architecture has been a primary aim.

In doing so, employees have more time to focus on the creative side of things, said OMA managing partner David Gianotten.

"What we see today is a growing portion of architectural practice involves verification – tasks that are increasingly logistical, repetitive, and time-consuming, often drawing energy away from design thinking," he said.

"For that reason, we actively encourage our teams to explore AI as a way to reduce these repetitive processes. By offloading administrative and verification tasks, AI allows architects to focus more on observation, critical thinking, and the formulation and development of ideas."

"AI is excellent for streamlining workflows and reducing the time our architects and designers spend on non‑creative tasks," corroborated Snøhetta's Mørseth.

Read:

Architects and engineers among professions most automatable by AI according to Anthropic

Beyond administrative tasks, studios are also integrating AI into their design workflows, with responses to Dezeen indicating adoption in every project stage, from inception through to delivery.

"We have AI tools that can be deployed across the entire project timeline, from conception to post-occupancy," Foster + Partners' Tsigkari and Eltarabishy said.

Eight studios we spoke to specified using AI for early-stage design development, including HOK.

According to the studio's senior principal, this process allows for more iterations in the concept phase – enhancing decision-making and creativity.

"We've found that these tools can accelerate decision-making and enhance collaboration for a more agile, creative, and insightful design process," said HOK's Breidenthal.

This is also true for head of digital office at White Arkitekter Peter Leuchovius, who said AI tools have made it easier to test initial ideas in collaboration with clients.

"We've improved customer dialogue by using generative AI in early-stage design – enabling us to faster visualise ideas, test multiple alternatives, and allow the client to participate more actively in the design work," said Leuchovius. "This has made collaboration faster, more informed, and more engaging."

"Making great imagery has never been easier"

Image generation was also among the most-popular tasks being supplemented by AI, reported by 16 of the 25 studios encouraging its use.

Typically outsourced to visualisation studios, architectural renderings are increasingly being realised in-house at a fraction of the time and cost with the help of AI tools.

This shift, according to principal and head of design at Hassell Xavier De Kestelier, is due to the simplicity of AI interfaces, which he argues allow just about anyone to use them.

"What AI does is democratise the process, empowering team members who may lack specialist technical rendering skills to produce highly sophisticated, high-end visualisations," De Kestelier claimed.

"Making great imagery has never been easier," Snøhetta's Mørseth added.

CF Møller estimated that its usage of image editing software Photoshop has fallen 80 per cent as a result of generative AI.

Other common uses of AI across the leading studios include project research, analysis and reports, data documentation, and modelling.

"We use AI and agent-based workflows to streamline labor-intensive coordination tasks such as documentation automation, data cleanup, computational design workflows, long-form document review, and custom software development," chief design technology officer at SOM Shane Burger added.

AI not "creative enough" to replace humans

While these AI tools are rapidly superseding existing systems, the studios highlight human creativity as one thing that cannot yet be replaced by technology.

"We've learned that AI excels at certain tasks, but doesn't pass muster for others," said MAD's Dahlen.

"Sometimes it can be clever and find connections that I hadn't thought about, other times it's just repetitive, inaccurate or not creative enough," she continued.

Managing partner at OMA David Gianotten and White Arkitekter's Peter Leuchovius share this sentiment.

"As a creative practice, we believe AI should enhance creative work rather than replace it," Gianotten told Dezeen.

"AI will never replace human creativity," Leuchovius added. "But handled right, it will for sure amplify it."

The top image is courtesy of Snøhetta.

item.content:encoded:
The Dezeen team was on the ground at Houghton Festival. Here are five standout installations from the festival, including a timber-and-thatch pavilion and a laser installation featuring a vintage campervan.

Set on the grounds of the historic Houghton Hall in Norfolk, England, the annual music festival featured an arts programme with new and returning commissions spanning sculpture, architecture, light and sound.

This roundup captured by the Dezeen team spotlights five of Houghton Festival's most interesting installations.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Dezeen (@dezeen)


The Dezeen team captured must-see installations at this year's festival

Among the installations was Water Tower, a timber-and-thatch pavilion designed by studios Cella Collective and Mitre & Mondays.

Informed by Houghton Hall's historic 1772 water tower, the structure was constructed using sustainably harvested reed from Scottish RSPB reedbeds, highlighting how regenerative design can support biodiversity and traditional craft.

After the event, the structure will be dismantled and reassembled each year as a recurring feature of the festival.

Another installation from the festival was Full Beam by light artist Chris Levine, a returning laser installation featuring a chrome-plated vintage Volkswagen campervan floating on the estate's lake.

Expanded from its 2025 debut at last year's festival, the work continued Levine's exploration of light and its ability to transform public space into "a moment of stillness."

Elsewhere, artists Nicole Gordon and Ke Peng's installation featured a suspended mirrored circle of rotating panels that playfully captured and redistributed a controlled beam of light, scattering reflections through the surrounding trees.

Another commission, by artist and DJ Call Super, took the form of an open-air living room constructed from felled trees from the Houghton estate. The exhibit explored the decline of communal "third places" and the rise of celebrity culture while inviting festival-goers to gather and interact.

Other festival installations featured on Dezeen include architectural installations from Burning Man 2025, standout pavilions from Glastonbury Festival and Benni Allan's suspended glowing canopy for last year's Houghton Festival.

Houghton Festival took place at Houghton Hall in Norfolk, England, from 6 to 9 August 2026, bringing together music, art, architecture and design across the historic estate.

item.content:encoded:
Undulating hills and winding rivers are translated into the letters of Vermont's updated tourism logo, designed by creative agency DNCO as part of a wider rebrand for the US state.

The Vermont Department of Tourism and Marketing asked DNCO to create a dedicated consumer tourism brand to reposition and strengthen awareness of the state, which is often overlooked in favour of other New England states like Maine and Massachusetts.

The agency formulated a brand platform around the tagline "State of Inspiration", which refers both to Vermont's natural beauty and to its creative energy, explained DNCO North America's managing director Luis Mendoza.

"The idea of a State of Inspiration captures what Vermont gives people," he told Dezeen.

"It might be learning a new skill, hearing an unexpected story or simply noticing the world differently. The identity presents Vermont not only as somewhere beautiful to visit, but as somewhere you leave having gained something."

A key element of the new identity is a logo based on the hand-painted signs found on roadsides, storefronts and farm stands across the state – a dramatic departure from its previous serif typeface.

The wordmark, which was developed in-house and refined by lettering artist Rob Clarke, features letterforms referencing aspects of Vermont's landscape, such as an 'e' that evokes a winding road, an 'm' that traces the outline of hills, and an 'o' that echoes the state administrative logo of a moon over mountains.

The brand identity utilises a single typeface in varying weights to adapt to different contexts. A colour palette that mirrors the natural environment can also change with the seasons, just like Vermont's landscape.

DNCO also developed a library of custom icons in collaboration with local illustrator Alyssa McCabe, references specific Vermont subjects including food, landscape, culture and local lore.

Mendoza hopes the "warm and playful" branding evokes not just the state's familiar qualities but also the unexpected experiences visitors may discover.

"We wanted the identity to feel unmistakably Vermont: rooted in the state's natural beauty and enduring charm, but also alive with creativity and possibility," he said.

Read:

Instagram redesigns its wordmark for first time in a decade

"There's a handmade quality to it that reflects the people and culture of the state, balanced with enough energy and flexibility to feel contemporary," Mendoza added

The State of Inspiration concept launched at the 2026 Vermont Tourism Summit. DNCO also developed brand guidelines and onboarding workshops to help roll out the identity across the state's marketing materials and collateral, including a refreshed tourism website.

"Our hope is that people see Vermont as more than a picturesque escape or a seasonal destination," Mendoza said.

"It is a place of discovery, creativity and new experiences, a place that can change your perspective and send you home feeling refreshed and inspired."

DNCO was founded in 2006 by Ben Dale and Joy Nazzari. Originally known as dn&co, the firm, which now has offices in New York and London, specialises in creating brands for global destinations including DUMBO in New York, St James's in London and Westbund Central in Shanghai.

Other branding projects recently featured on Dezeen include the updated wordmark for social media platform Instagram and a rebranded badge for Lisbon football club.

The images are courtesy of DNCO.

item.content:encoded:
Local design-build studio Allprace aimed to create a feeling of "warmth and permanence" in a house called Hargis, which features gabled roof forms and earthy materials such as wood and stone.

Set within a creative district in Culver City, which is part of Los Angeles County, the project was designed for a client who "values understated luxury, exceptional craftsmanship, and a lifestyle centred around art, nature and walkability," said Allprace.

It is located on a rectangular property that formerly held an ageing house and two-car garage, which were demolished.

In their place, the team created a main residence and a detached guesthouse. Rather than creating a sense of "luxury through excess", the team sought to design a calm, restorative house that was connected to its surroundings.

"Throughout the redesign, founder Shanty and her partner James Mulyadi focused on creating a residence where every material contributes to a sense of warmth and permanence," the team said.

The main dwelling is topped with a prominent roof consisting of gabled and flat elements. Facades are clad in wood and light-toned brick.

The ground level holds an open-concept kitchen, dining area and living room, along with a bedroom and garage.

The upper floor contains bedrooms and a den, and is designed to have a "quieter, more intimate atmosphere dedicated to rest".

In the rear yard, there is a guest house and a small swimming pool, a portion of which is sheltered by the structure's upper level.

Influenced by the concept of biophilia, the architecture studio picked earthy materials such as stone, wood and living plants. An emphasis was placed on craftsmanship and expressing the texture of materials.

Read:

B2A Architects uses concrete columns to elevate Dutch home above dyke

The ground level features limestone flooring, while the upper level has herringbone-patterned wood flooring. The kitchen is fitted with a travertine island and white oak cabinetry.

Notable lighting fixtures include a Bocci chandelier from its 14 Series, which is suspended above a spiral staircase.

Rooms feature custom millwork and ample glazing, including a large triangular window in the primary bathroom.

"One of the home's defining architectural moments is a dramatic, 14-foot by 20-foot triangular window, which floods the interiors with natural light while creating a sculptural focal point visible from both inside and out," the team said.

Other projects in Culver City include a faceted, courtyard-style house by FreelandBuck and a bungalow renovation by Edward Ogosta, which features an extension with a window wall and angled roof.

The photography is by Gavin Cater.

item.content:encoded:
A skyscraper-sized jail designed by architecture studio HOK is undergoing site preparation in New York City's Chinatown as one of the four new borough-based structures designed to replace the city's notorious Rikers Island jail complex.

The Manhattan Detention Facility will be located at 125 White Street in Chinatown, on the same site as the former Manhattan Detention Complex (The Tombs), which was demolished in 2024.

The most up-to-date renders released by the New York City Department of Design and Construction (DDC) and HOK show a building that is 335 feet tall (102 metres) and roughly 13 floors, which aligns with the height of the New York County Criminal Court building next door.

It will be the tallest correctional facility in the world if built to this height, leading to its being dubbed a "jailscraper".

The Manhattan Detention Facility building is split into two main volumes by a walkway that cuts through the bottom of the base and provides a pedestrian passageway across the site.

A reddish mesh screen and undulating panels cover a portion of the facade.

Towards the middle of the building, this "double skin system with security mesh" will act as a viewpoint for those in custody and surround spaces such as the "recreation hall".

"To address privacy, a double skin system with security mesh and architectural screen supports visual privacy by creating a separation between the exterior-most facade and the people in custody," reads a DDC design document.

Cells are located in the upper floors, while the ground level will contain a public lobby, a community and retail space and a staff lobby. Below ground, there will be parking for Department of Correction and New York Police Department staff.

A total of 1,040 beds are planned for the facility.

Read:

Bronx jail designed to be "responsive to the neighborhood"

According to the DDC, the city is still working with the surrounding community and the architecture team to finalise the design, which is updated periodically on the project website.

Per community request, a variety of plantings and some seating will be placed around the site and in the public walkway.

A visitor space that "feels comfortable and supports a welcoming environment" and contains easily accessible lockers and restrooms is also planned for the building per the community's request, according to the DDC.

An assortment of public artwork that previously surrounded the Tombs will be preserved and integrated around the site.

This includes aluminium wire sculptures by artist Kit-Yin Snyder, which stood outside the former entrance, and stone bas-reliefs by Richard Hass, which were encapsulated in the old facade.

Site work on the new Manhattan Detention Facility is underway, including utility work and preliminary excavation. It is slated for completion in 2032.

The jail is one of four in New York City put forward to receive a relocated population from the Rikers Island jail complex. Rikers Island, a small island located in the East River, contains 10 of the city's 15 correctional facilities, which hold up to 15,000 detainees.

It is notorious for its violent environment and inhumane conditions.

In 2019, New York City announced the complex's eventual closure, with plans to disperse the incarcerated population into four smaller jails in Manhattan, Brooklyn, The Bronx and Queens via an initiative called the Borough-Based Jail Program.

HOK is leading the design of the Manhattan and Brooklyn jails, with Cetra Ruddy on The Bronx project and Michael Graves and others on the Queens jail.

Work on all four facilities is underway and in various stages, with the Brooklyn jail the furthest along, topping out just short of the Manhattan jail's planned height at 295 feet (89 metres).

Read:

Nordic model to inform redesign of California's San Quentin prison

The Manhattan jail has drawn much controversy, with the public and community organisations in opposition. Most recently, local leaders penned a letter to New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, warning of the site's structural fragility and calling for a reevaluation of the location.

"If foundation problems on this site delay or derail construction of the Manhattan facility, the four-borough program cannot absorb the Rikers population and closing Rikers will slip further out of reach," it reads.

Renderings of the Bronx Detention Center by CetraRuddy were made public last year. It is designed to be "responsive to the neighbourhood" and is made up of a stepped volume wrapped in a similar mesh screen as the Manhattan complex.

Some architecture studios have said that design can aid in creating more humane conditions for those incarcerated, while others, such as architect Michael Ford, have called on the design community to stop designing jails and prisons outright.

The images are by HOK, courtesy of the New York City Department of Design and Construction.

item.content:encoded:
Indian studio Evolving Radical Aesthetics has completed Ushas, a farmhouse built into a steep Kerala hillside with an open-air temple carved into a retaining wall.

Located in the Malabar hills near Kozhikode, the house was designed for a retired couple who relocated from Andhra Pradesh to cultivate farmland after leaving city life behind.

The home is organised as three staggered volumes, inspired by the region's traditional farmhouses, and positioned to follow the site's contours rather than level them.

"The terrain became our datum. It dictated orientation, levels, movement, structural logic, even materiality," Evolving Radical Aesthetics principal architect and partner Muhammed Ashiqe told Dezeen.

"It's not every day you come across a site so surreal you lose your sense of place," landscape architect and partner AR Rumna said.

"To build is, in itself, an act of harm, so we thought about what was needed and to what extent an untouched piece of land should be disturbed," Rumna continued. "We wanted to build with minimum impact to the site."

The house is built from locally sourced black granite stone laid in thick masonry walls. Above them, a roof made from corrugated galvanised steel sheets, slender steel rafters and traditional Mangalore tiles extends outwards to shelter verandahs from Kerala's heavy monsoon rain.

"We built with locally sourced black granite," Rumna said. "The wall-making imitated the act of cave building – a very basic, primal form of shelter."

"We wanted the house to feel like it's one with the ground, while the light roof ensures that we don't impose anything that would stand out. We wanted the hills to be in the foreground."

A passage running between the stone volumes forms the main route through the house, connecting living spaces, bedrooms and the surrounding farmland.

The passage also leads to a dedicated room for reading and practising the veena – a stringed Indian instrument – which has glazed walls that open directly onto the landscape.

Read:

Summer Home by Mindspark Architects overlooks cardamom plantation in India

Shelters for farm workers sit alongside the main route through the house, reflecting its role as both a home and working farmhouse.

Large openings frame views across the landscape, while verandahs supported by slender metal columns extend the rooms outdoors.

The bedrooms open directly onto sheltered terraces overlooking the hillside, while the living spaces look across the surrounding mountains through full-height glazing beneath the pitched roof.

The building was angled to capture prevailing north-eastern winds, with the granite walls helping to keep the interiors cool.

"Deep overhangs protect the house from rain and sun and also create verandahs to sit out and relax," Ashiqe said.

The steep site's high winds also presented a risk to the Mangalore tiles, so the architects placed a layer of corrugated galvanised steel beneath them to prevent the tiles from breaking or being lifted.

The concealed layer also channels rainwater towards the eaves for drainage.

At the lower level of the site, outside the main house, square-cut granite steps descend to an open-air temple set into the retaining wall.

The living room projects over the shrine above, creating a cantilevered sheltered space for meditation with a stone podium facing the mountains.

"The temple being carved into the retaining wall with the living room cantilevered above is reminiscent of cave temples, a space for solitude and meditation," Rumna said.

"There is also a podium to dance against the backdrop of the mountains, as an offering to the deity."

The surrounding landscape continues the contours of the site with stepped planting beds and walking paths.

Initially built on largely barren ground, the gardens have gradually been planted by the owners with native trees, vegetables and tropical planting, allowing the farmhouse to evolve alongside the land.

Founded by Ashiqe in 2012, Evolving Radical Aesthetics is an architecture studio based in Kozhikode, Kerala.

The practice focuses primarily on residential architecture and projects rooted in local climate, materials and topography.

Other homes in Kerala featured on Dezeen include Mindspark Architects' Summer Home, which overlooks a cardamom plantation and opens onto two timber viewing decks through glazed sliding doors.

Another Kerala home that makes use of Mangalore tiles is Ananda by Thought Parallels Architecture, which features a palette of red brickwork, teak wood and carved fretwork panels under an oversized coconut-wood roof.

The photography is by Syam Sreesylam.

item.content:encoded:
Pritzker Prize-winning architect Shigeru Ban has completed a wellness hotel on Awaji Island, Japan.

Named the Pasona Natureverse Retreat, the hotel at the tip of Awaji Island near Kobe was designed for long-term stays based on the ideal of Mibyo – an ideal of preventive wellness treatment that translates as "pre-illness".

The hotel is the third project designed by Ban for Japanese company Pasona Group on the island. It follows a thatch-topped restaurant and a wooden meditation retreat.

According to Ban, the hotel's D-shaped form was designed to take advantage of its location between the coast and a forest.

"To express the characteristics of a site defined by these two completely contrasting landscapes, distinct facades were designed for the east and west sides," said Ban.

"Two linear structures with individual qualities are integrated into a single D-shaped plan, flanking a light-filled atrium."

The five-storey hotel was designed primarily for long-term, 30-day-plus retreats, as well as offering shorter stays.

Its 57 rooms are arranged around a large, skylit central atrium with half overlooking the sea and half facing the forest.

While the landward facade is adorned with stylised timber columns, the seaward side was designed to express horizontally, with balconies running the full width on all levels.

"On the seaside, using the seawall as a podium, the facade is highly transparent, featuring four levels of emphasised horizontal slabs that create a seamless continuity between the interior, exterior, and the surrounding scenery," said Ban.

"In contrast to the horizontal emphasis of the seaside, the mountain-side facade features a rhythmic arrangement of timber-clad columns that emphasize a symbolic, somewhat classical vertical structure," he continued.

"At the center, a massive timber canopy and a grand staircase welcome visitors."

Stays at the hotel are focused on preventive wellness treatments, with all guests receiving a personalised wellness program that may include thalassotherapy, hammam meditation, yoga, sound therapy and aromatherapy.

Every room in the hotel contains a private onsen – a natural hot spring bath – and several rooms have sensor-operated beds that monitor nighttime body movement and adjust automatically to encourage the best sleep.

Read:

Shigeru Ban creates wooden Zenbo Seinei retreat on Japanese island

Along with a wellness clinic and treatment room, the hotel includes a dedicated room for aerial yoga with suspended fabric hammocks and a gym.

An indoor swimming pool is fed with salt water from the Seto Inland Sea.

Alongside the wellness facilities, the hotel contains five restaurants, several run by Michelin-starred chefs, as well as several cafes.

On the third floor, an event hall was designed for live musical performances and contains 500 window panes covered in artworks.

One of the world's most respected architects, Ban won the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2014 and was recently awarded the 2026 AIA Gold Medal.

He is known for his innovative architecture that often uses cardboard and natural materials, with the Cardboard Cathedral in Christchurch one of his most influential buildings.

The photography is by Hiroyuki Hirai.

item.content:encoded:
Design studios Cella Collective and Mitre & Mondays have designed a timber-framed installation for this year's Houghton Festival in Norfolk, England, covering its walls with thatch sourced from sustainable reedbeds.

Named the Water Tower, the installation provided a restful seating space between the food area and one of the stages at the music and arts event Houghton Festival, which took place from 6 to 9 August.

Cella Collective and Mitre & Mondays' design for the 5.5-metre-tall installation drew upon a water tower built for the nearby Houghton Hall in 1772.

Made from a timber frame, the installation featured four openings separated by slanted walls that were covered in layers of thatch.

A thatched ring topped the structure and wooden seating extended from the walls inside, where visitors could view the circular roof opening above.

"I want people to experience something that looks like it has grown out of the ground – to feel cooled by its shady interior, to feel a connection to it when checking out its handmade flavour," Mitre & Mondays co-founder Josef Shanley-Jackson told Dezeen.

"Thatched structures, inside and out, can feel both contemporary and old-feeling all at the same time," added Cella Collective member Alys Hargreaves.

"It makes sense that we should be revisiting it as a building material which offers a great solution for climate cooling both in the growing of the material and the built structure."

The studios were motivated by regenerative design principles when creating the Water Tower.

The thatch material used in the installation was sourced from reedbeds managed by the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB), utilising a by-product material from RSPB's land cutting, which in turn supports the group's conservation efforts and the local wildlife.

Read:

Cob can be "a mainstream building material once again" say Cella

"We centred the whole design around a material ecosystem – reedbed landscapes and the craft of thatching – which aims to support our environment and local building cultures, both of which are under threat or in decline in their own ways," said Hargreaves.

"It has also been an exercise in opposing a culture of convenience where you can only easily buy off-the-shelf items that are part of global supply chains," she continued. "We wanted to learn how we might challenge this and embrace a new material in all its entirety."

Cella Collective and Mitre & Mondays consulted with Cheshire-based master thatchers Wayne Halfpenny and Steve Kelly on the thatching.

"We adopted their intuitive process of crafting with thatch, adapting the design to accommodate the reed," said Cella Collective member Ella Caldicott. "That intuition became part of the build process, with decisions often made through testing and adapting to what was in front of us."

"You can't learn that from reading books; you learn it through your hands and eyes – that's why collaborating with craftsmen and craftswomen is so valuable."

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Dezeen (@dezeen)


The thatching was made from reeds sourced from RSPB-managed reedbeds

The Water Tower will be disassembled and reinstalled for future editions of Houghton Festival. Other installations at the festival included a glowing canopy suspended from the trees, which was designed last year by EBBA Architects founder Benni Allan.

We recently rounded up nine contemporary buildings with thatched roofs from around the world, indicating a revival of the age-old craft.

The photography is by Henry Woide.
